questions.q: Which of the following constitutional provisions deals with the appointment, tenure, and responsibility of the Central Council of Ministers?
questions.e: While Article 74 deals with the status of the council of ministers (to aid and advise the President), Article 75 specifically deals with the appointment, tenure, responsibility, qualification, oath, and salaries and allowances of the ministers.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding the size of the Council of Ministers: 1️⃣ The total number of ministers, including the Prime Minister, cannot exceed 15% of the total strength of the Lok Sabha. 2️⃣ This provision was added to the Constitution by the 44th Amendment Act of 1978.
questions.e: According to Article 75, the total number of ministers, including the Prime Minister, shall not exceed 15% of the total strength of the Lok Sabha. This provision was added by the 91st Amendment Act of 2003, not the 44th.

questions.q: According to the Constitution, a minister who is not a member of either House of Parliament for any consecutive period of ________ shall cease to be a minister.
questions.e: Article 75(5) states that a minister who for any period of six consecutive months is not a member of either House of Parliament shall at the expiration of that period cease to be a minister.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding the relationship between the President and the Council of Ministers: 1️⃣ The President is bound to act in accordance with the advice tendered by the Council of Ministers. 2️⃣ The President can require the Council of Ministers to reconsider such advice only once. 3️⃣ The nature of advice tendered by ministers to the President cannot be inquired into in any court.
questions.e: Under Article 74, the President must act in accordance with the advice of the Council of Ministers. The 44th Amendment allows the President to ask for reconsideration once, but he must follow the advice given after such reconsideration. Article 74(2) bars courts from inquiring into the advice.

questions.q: Which Article of the Constitution states that all executive action of the Government of India shall be expressed to be taken in the name of the President?
questions.e: Article 77 deals with the conduct of business of the Government of India. It specifies that all executive actions shall be expressed to be taken in the name of the President and that the President shall make rules for the allocation of business among ministers.

questions.q: With reference to the duties of the Prime Minister under Article 78, which of the following are included? 1️⃣ To communicate to the President all decisions of the Council of Ministers. 2️⃣ To furnish information relating to the administration of the Union as the President may call for. 3️⃣ To submit for consideration of the Council any matter on which a decision has been taken by a minister but not considered by the Council.
questions.e: Article 78 defines the duties of the Prime Minister as a bridge between the Cabinet and the President. It includes communicating all decisions, furnishing requested information, and submitting individual ministerial decisions for Council consideration if the President so requires.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding the rights of ministers in Parliament: 1️⃣ Every minister has the right to speak and take part in the proceedings of either House. 2️⃣ A minister can vote in both Houses of Parliament. 3️⃣ A minister who is a member of the Rajya Sabha can participate in the proceedings of the Lok Sabha.
questions.e: Under Article 88, every minister has the right to speak and take part in the proceedings of either House, any joint sitting, and any committee of which he/she is a member. However, a minister is entitled to vote only in the House of which he/she is a member.

questions.q: In which of the following cases did the Supreme Court hold that the President cannot exercise executive power without the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers, even after the dissolution of the Lok Sabha?
questions.e: In the U.N.R. Rao vs. Indira Gandhi case (1971), the Supreme Court held that Article 74 is mandatory and the Council of Ministers does not cease to hold office even after the dissolution of the Lok Sabha; therefore, the President must always have a Council to advise him.

questions.q: Which Constitutional Amendment Act made the advice of the Council of Ministers binding on the President?
questions.e: The 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act of 1976 amended Article 74 to state that the President shall, in the exercise of his functions, act in accordance with the advice rendered by the Council of Ministers.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding the appointment of ministers: 1️⃣ The Prime Minister is appointed by the President. 2️⃣ Other ministers are appointed by the President on the advice of the Prime Minister. 3️⃣ The President has the discretion to appoint any person as a minister without the Prime Minister's recommendation.
questions.e: The Prime Minister is appointed by the President. However, for other ministers, the President can only appoint persons recommended by the Prime Minister. This means the President has no discretion in the choice of other ministers.

questions.q: What is the "oath of secrecy" taken by a Union Minister?
o: To do right to all manner of people without fear or favor
To bear true faith and allegiance to the Constitution
To uphold the sovereignty and integrity of India
To not reveal any matter brought under consideration as a minister except for due discharge of duties
questions.e: The oath of secrecy involves the minister swearing that he/she will not directly or indirectly communicate or reveal any matter known to him/her as a Union minister except as required for the due discharge of his/her duties.

questions.q: The principle of "Collective Responsibility" implies that: 1️⃣ All ministers are jointly responsible to the Lok Sabha for their acts. 2️⃣ If the Lok Sabha passes a no-confidence motion, only the ministers from the Lok Sabha must resign. 3️⃣ Cabinet decisions bind all ministers even if they differed in the meeting.
questions.e: Collective responsibility means ministers "swim or sink together." If a no-confidence motion passes, the entire council, including Rajya Sabha members, must resign. It also means all ministers must support cabinet decisions publicly or resign.

questions.q: Who stated that "Collective responsibility can be achieved only through the instrumentality of the Prime Minister"?
questions.e: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar observed in the Constituent Assembly that collective responsibility is impossible without the Prime Minister having the statutory authority to nominate and dismiss ministers.

questions.q: Unlike Britain, in India: 1️⃣ There is no system of legal responsibility of a minister. 2️⃣ An order of the President for a public act does not need to be countersigned by a minister. 3️⃣ The courts can enquire into the nature of advice rendered by ministers to the President.
questions.e: In Britain, ministers countersign royal orders and are legally responsible in court. In India, there is no legal responsibility; presidential orders don't need countersignatures, and courts are barred from inquiring into ministerial advice (Article 74).

questions.q: Match the following categories of ministers with their descriptions: 1️⃣ Cabinet Ministers: Head important ministries like Home and Defence. 2️⃣ Ministers of State: Always have independent charge of departments. 3️⃣ Deputy Ministers: Attached to Cabinet Ministers to assist them.
questions.e: Cabinet ministers head major ministries. Ministers of State can either have independent charge or be attached to cabinet ministers. Deputy ministers are always attached to senior ministers to assist in administrative and parliamentary duties; they never have independent charge.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a member of the Council of Ministers?
questions.e: The Council of Ministers consists of Cabinet Ministers, Ministers of State, and Deputy Ministers. Parliamentary Secretaries are a separate category; they are appointed by the PM, not the President, and are not members of the Council.

questions.q: Consider the differences between the Council of Ministers and the Cabinet: 1️⃣ The Council of Ministers is a wider body, while the Cabinet is a smaller part of it. 2️⃣ The term 'Cabinet' was present in the original text of the Constitution. 3️⃣ The Cabinet meets as a body to take policy decisions, while the Council of Ministers does not.
questions.e: The Cabinet consists of only Cabinet-rank ministers and is a sub-part of the larger Council. The term 'Cabinet' was not in the original Constitution; it was inserted into Article 352 by the 44th Amendment in 1978.

questions.q: Which body is described as the "steering wheel of the ship of the state" or the "pivot around which the whole political machinery revolves"?
questions.e: Various political scientists like Ramsay Muir and Sir John Marriott have described the Cabinet as the central directing instrument, the "steering wheel," or the "pivot" of the government due to its supreme decision-making power.

questions.q: What is the "Kitchen Cabinet" in the Indian context?
o: The panel of chairpersons in the Lok Sabha
A committee that manages the PM's household
An informal body consisting of the PM and a few influential colleagues
A formal committee of the Council of Ministers dealing with food security
questions.e: The 'Kitchen Cabinet' or 'Inner Cabinet' is an informal, extra-constitutional body consisting of the PM and 2-4 influential colleagues/friends whom the PM trusts. It is the real center of power where crucial decisions are often made.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding Cabinet Committees: 1️⃣ They are mentioned in the Constitution of India. 2️⃣ They are set up by the Prime Minister. 3️⃣ They can take decisions that are subject to review by the Cabinet.
questions.e: Cabinet Committees are extra-constitutional (not in the Constitution). They are set up by the PM according to the needs of the time. They help reduce the Cabinet's workload and can take decisions, though the Cabinet can review them.

questions.q: Which Cabinet Committee is often described as a "Super-Cabinet"?
questions.e: The Cabinet Committee on Political Affairs is the most powerful committee as it deals with all policy matters pertaining to domestic and foreign affairs.

questions.q: At present, how many Cabinet Committees are functional in India?
questions.e: According to the provided text, there are 8 functional Cabinet Committees, including those on Political Affairs, Economic Affairs, Security, and Investment and Growth.

questions.q: Which Cabinet Committee deals with issues relating to atomic energy and internal security?
questions.e: The Cabinet Committee on Security is specifically tasked with issues relating to defence, law and order, internal security, and atomic energy.

questions.q: What are "Groups of Ministers" (GoMs)?
o: Permanent sub-committees of the Rajya Sabha
Ad hoc bodies formed to give recommendations to the Cabinet on emergent issues
Formal committees mentioned in the Constitution
A group of private members who advise the President
questions.e: GoMs are ad hoc bodies constituted to look into specific issues and provide recommendations to the Cabinet. Some are empowered to take decisions, while others are purely advisory. They are disbanded once their task is complete.

questions.q: Which of the following parts of the Constitution deal with the organization and powers of the Parliament?
questions.e: Articles 79 to 122 in Part V of the Constitution deal with the organization, composition, duration, officers, procedures, privileges, and powers of the Parliament.

questions.q: The Parliament of India consists of which of the following? 1️⃣ The President. 2️⃣ The Council of States. 3️⃣ The House of the People. 4️⃣ The Vice-President.
questions.e: Under the Constitution, the Parliament of India consists of three parts: the President, the Rajya Sabha (Council of States), and the Lok Sabha (House of the People). Though the President is not a member of either House, he is an integral part of Parliament.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding the Rajya Sabha: 1️⃣ Its maximum strength is fixed at 250. 2️⃣ 12 members are nominated by the President from fields like art and science. 3️⃣ Representatives of states are elected by the people through direct election.
questions.e: The Rajya Sabha's max strength is 250 (238 elected, 12 nominated). Representatives of states are elected indirectly by the elected members of state legislative assemblies, not by direct election.

questions.q: Which Schedule of the Constitution deals with the allocation of seats in the Rajya Sabha?
questions.e: The Fourth Schedule of the Constitution of India deals with the allocation of seats in the Rajya Sabha to the states and union territories.

questions.q: How are representatives of Union Territories in the Rajya Sabha chosen?
o: Through direct election by the people
Through indirect election by an electoral college specially constituted for this purpose
questions.e: Representatives of each Union Territory in the Rajya Sabha are indirectly elected by members of an electoral college specially constituted for the purpose.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding the Lok Sabha: 1️⃣ The maximum strength is fixed at 550. 2️⃣ Voting age was reduced from 21 to 18 years by the 61st Amendment Act. 3️⃣ Two Anglo-Indian members are still nominated by the President as of 2024.
questions.e: The Lok Sabha's max strength is 550 (530 states, 20 UTs). The 61st Amendment reduced the voting age to 18. The provision for nominating two Anglo-Indians was discontinued by the 104th Amendment Act of 2019, effective from January 2020.

questions.q: What is the "First-Past-The-Post" system used for in India?
questions.e: For the Lok Sabha, India uses the system of territorial representation or the "First-Past-The-Post" system, where the candidate who secures a simple majority of votes in a single-member constituency is declared elected.

questions.q: Why did the Constitution not adopt proportional representation for Lok Sabha elections? 1️⃣ It is difficult for illiterate voters to understand the complicated system. 2️⃣ It tends to multiply political parties, leading to instability. 3️⃣ It is highly expensive.
questions.e: Proportional representation was rejected for Lok Sabha because of its complexity for a then-largely illiterate electorate, its tendency to cause government instability by multiplying parties, its high cost, and the fact that it eliminates contact between voters and representatives.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding the duration of the Houses: 1️⃣ The Rajya Sabha is a continuing chamber and not subject to dissolution. 2️⃣ The normal term of the Lok Sabha is six years. 3️⃣ One-third of Rajya Sabha members retire every second year.
questions.e: The Rajya Sabha is a permanent body; its members serve for 6 years, with 1/3 retiring every 2nd year. The Lok Sabha is not a continuing chamber and has a normal term of 5 years.

questions.q: During a National Emergency, the term of the Lok Sabha can be extended by a law of Parliament for:
o: One year at a time for any length of time
questions.e: During a national emergency, Parliament can extend the Lok Sabha's term for one year at a time for any length of time. However, this extension cannot continue beyond six months after the emergency has ceased to operate.

questions.q: To be eligible for election as a member of the Rajya Sabha, a person must be not less than ________ years of age.
questions.e: The Constitution specifies that a person must be at least 30 years of age to be a member of the Rajya Sabha and at least 25 years of age for the Lok Sabha.

questions.q: Under the Tenth Schedule, who decides the question of disqualification of a member of Parliament on the ground of defection?
o: The Presiding Officer of the House
questions.e: Unlike other disqualifications (decided by the President), the question of disqualification under the Tenth Schedule (Anti-Defection Law) is decided by the Chairman in the Rajya Sabha and the Speaker in the Lok Sabha.

questions.q: A member of Parliament vacates his/her seat if he/she is absent from all meetings of the House without permission for a period of:
questions.e: According to Article 101, a House can declare a seat vacant if the member is absent from all its meetings for a period of sixty days without permission.

questions.q: What is the "effective majority" required for the removal of the Speaker of the Lok Sabha?
o: Majority of all the then members of the House (excluding vacancies)
Majority of members present and voting
Majority of the total membership of the House
Two-thirds majority of members present and voting
questions.e: An "effective majority" means a majority of the total membership of the House excluding vacant seats. This is required for the removal of the Speaker, Deputy Speaker, and the Vice-President (in Rajya Sabha).

questions.q: Who administers the oath or affirmation to a member of Parliament?
o: The President or some person appointed by him
questions.e: Every member of Parliament must take an oath or affirmation before the President or some person appointed by him/her for this purpose before taking their seat in the House.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding the Speaker of the Lok Sabha: 1️⃣ He/she is elected by the Lok Sabha from amongst its members. 2️⃣ He/she vacates office immediately when the Lok Sabha is dissolved. 3️⃣ He/she does not vote in the first instance but has a casting vote in case of a tie.
questions.e: The Speaker is elected by the House. He/she does not vacate office on dissolution but continues until the newly-elected Lok Sabha meets. He/she only votes in the event of an equality of votes (casting vote).

questions.q: Which of the following powers are unique to the Speaker of Lok Sabha and not shared by the Chairman of Rajya Sabha? 1️⃣ Deciding whether a bill is a Money Bill. 2️⃣ Presiding over a joint sitting of both Houses. 3️⃣ Exercising a casting vote.
questions.e: The Speaker has two special powers: final authority to certify a bill as a Money Bill and presiding over joint sittings. Both the Speaker and Chairman exercise casting votes.

questions.q: The "Quorum" to constitute a meeting of either House of Parliament is:
questions.e: Quorum is the minimum number of members required to be present to transact business. In India, it is one-tenth of the total number of members in each House, including the presiding officer.

questions.q: What is "Adjournment Sine Die"?
o: Terminating a sitting for a specified number of hours
Terminating a sitting of Parliament for an indefinite period
Terminating a session of the House
questions.e: Adjournment sine die means terminating a sitting of Parliament without naming a day for reassembly. This is done by the presiding officer.

questions.q: Consider the differences between Adjournment and Prorogation: 1️⃣ Adjournment terminates a sitting, while Prorogation terminates a session. 2️⃣ Adjournment is done by the Presiding Officer, while Prorogation is done by the President. 3️⃣ Neither affects the bills pending before the House.
questions.e: Adjournment only pauses a sitting; Prorogation ends the entire session. Adjournment is the Presiding Officer's power, while Prorogation is the President's. In India, neither causes pending bills to lapse.

questions.q: Which of the following bills does NOT lapse on the dissolution of the Lok Sabha?
o: A bill originating in the Lok Sabha but transmitted to the Rajya Sabha
A bill passed by the Lok Sabha but pending in the Rajya Sabha
A bill pending in the Lok Sabha
A bill pending in the Rajya Sabha but not passed by the Lok Sabha
questions.e: A bill that is pending in the Rajya Sabha but has not been passed by the Lok Sabha does not lapse. Conversely, any bill pending in the Lok Sabha or passed by it but pending in the Rajya Sabha will lapse.

questions.q: What is the "Lame-duck session" of Parliament?
o: The last session of an existing Lok Sabha after a new one has been elected
A session called to discuss an emergency
The first session of a new Lok Sabha
The session where the budget is passed
questions.e: A lame-duck session refers to the last session of the preceding Lok Sabha after the results of the new Lok Sabha elections are out but before the new House is constituted. "Lame-ducks" are those who failed to get re-elected.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding the types of majorities: 1️⃣ Absolute Majority is a majority of the total membership of the House. 2️⃣ Special Majority for constitutional amendment (Article 368) requires 2/3rd of members present and voting and a majority of total strength. 3️⃣ Impeachment of the President requires a simple majority.
questions.e: Absolute majority refers to more than 50% of the total strength. Article 368 requires a "double majority" (majority of total + 2/3rd of present/voting). Impeachment (Article 61) requires a much tougher 2/3rd majority of the *total* membership of the House.

questions.q: What is "Zero Hour" in Indian parliamentary proceedings?
o: The final hour of a session
The hour dedicated to voting on the budget
The time when the House is dissolved
The time gap between Question Hour and the regular agenda
questions.e: Zero Hour is an informal device (not in the Rules of Procedure) where members can raise urgent matters. It starts immediately after Question Hour and is an Indian innovation in parliamentary procedure since 1962.

questions.q: Match the following types of closure motions: 1️⃣ Kangaroo Closure: Only important clauses are discussed; intervening ones are skipped. 2️⃣ Guillotine Closure: Undiscussed clauses are put to vote due to want of time. 3️⃣ Simple Closure: Member moves that the matter has been sufficiently discussed.
questions.e: All three are correctly matched. Closure motions are used to cut short debates. Kangaroo closure focuses on key points, while Guillotine is used when time runs out for the entire bill.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding "No-Confidence Motion": 1️⃣ It can be moved in both the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha. 2️⃣ It needs the support of 50 members to be admitted in the Lok Sabha. 3️⃣ If passed, the entire Council of Ministers must resign.
questions.e: A no-confidence motion can only be introduced in the Lok Sabha (due to collective responsibility). It requires 50 supporters for admission. If passed, the government falls and must resign.

questions.q: What is a "Money Bill" as per Article 110 of the Constitution?
o: A bill dealing with the imposition, abolition, or regulation of any tax
Any bill that involves government spending
A bill passed by a joint sitting of both Houses
A bill that amends the fundamental rights
questions.e: Under Article 110, a bill is a Money Bill if it deals *only* with specific fiscal matters like taxes, government borrowing, or the Consolidated Fund. The Speaker's decision on this is final.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding the legislative procedure for a Money Bill: 1️⃣ It can be introduced in either House of Parliament. 2️⃣ The Rajya Sabha must return it within 14 days. 3️⃣ The President can return it for reconsideration.
questions.e: Money Bills can only be introduced in the Lok Sabha on the President's recommendation. Rajya Sabha has very limited powers and must return it in 14 days. The President can approve or withhold assent but *cannot* return it for reconsideration.

questions.q: Which of the following is true about "Financial Bills (I)"?
o: They are identical to Money Bills in all respects
They require the recommendation of the President for introduction
They cannot be amended by the Rajya Sabha
They can be introduced in either House
questions.e: Financial Bills (I) under Article 117(1) are similar to Money Bills in that they only start in the Lok Sabha and need the PM's recommendation. However, they are like ordinary bills in other respects, meaning Rajya Sabha *can* amend or reject them.

questions.q: When can a "Joint Sitting" of both Houses be summoned?
o: To resolve a deadlock over an Ordinary Bill
questions.e: Article 108 provides for a joint sitting only for Ordinary or Financial Bills to resolve deadlocks. It is *not* applicable to Money Bills (Lok Sabha dominates) or Constitution Amendment Bills (must pass separately).

questions.q: Who presides over a joint sitting of the two Houses of Parliament?
questions.e: The Speaker of the Lok Sabha presides over a joint sitting. In his/her absence, the Deputy Speaker presides, and if he/she is also absent, the Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha presides. The Chairman of Rajya Sabha *never* presides.

questions.q: The Constitution refers to the "Budget" as:
questions.e: The term 'budget' is not used in the Constitution. Article 112 refers to it as the 'annual financial statement', which is a statement of estimated receipts and expenditure for the financial year.

questions.q: Which of the following expenditures is "Charged" on the Consolidated Fund of India and therefore non-votable?
o: Salaries and allowances of the Speaker of Lok Sabha
questions.e: "Charged" expenditures are non-votable; they can be discussed but not voted upon. These include the salaries of the President, Speaker, Deputy Speaker, Chairman, Deputy Chairman, and Supreme Court judges.

questions.q: Consider the stages in the enactment of the Budget: 1️⃣ Presentation of Budget. 2️⃣ General Discussion. 3️⃣ Voting on demands for grants. 4️⃣ Passing of Appropriation Bill.
questions.e: The budget goes through six stages: Presentation, General Discussion, Scrutiny by Departmental Committees, Voting on Demands for Grants (Lok Sabha only), Passing of Appropriation Bill, and Passing of Finance Bill.

questions.q: What is "Guillotine" in the context of the Budget?
o: A motion to reject the entire budget
A specific type of economy cut motion
Putting all remaining demands for grants to vote on the last day, whether discussed or not
A physical tool used to stop a member from speaking
questions.e: Guillotine is the procedure where the Speaker puts all outstanding demands for grants to vote on the last day allotted for discussion, regardless of whether they have been debated.

questions.q: What is a "Vote on Account"?
o: A vote to impeach the President
A final vote on the Appropriation Bill
A grant made in advance by the Lok Sabha to cover expenditure for a part of the year
A vote of thanks to the President
questions.e: Since the budget enactment takes time, the Constitution allows the Lok Sabha to make a 'Vote on Account'—a grant in advance—to enable the government to function until the Appropriation Act is passed.

questions.q: Which of the following funds is operated by executive action and does not require parliamentary appropriation for payments?
questions.e: While the Consolidated Fund requires a law for withdrawal, the Public Account and the Contingency Fund of India are operated by executive action. The Contingency Fund is at the President's disposal for unforeseen expenses.

questions.q: The Rajya Sabha has equal status with the Lok Sabha in which of the following matters? 1️⃣ Election and impeachment of the President. 2️⃣ Removal of the Vice-President. 3️⃣ Voting on demands for grants.
questions.e: Rajya Sabha is equal to Lok Sabha in presidential elections/impeachment and starting the removal of the VP. However, it has no power to vote on demands for grants; that is an exclusive privilege of the Lok Sabha.

questions.q: Consider the "Special Powers" of the Rajya Sabha: 1️⃣ Authorizing Parliament to make laws on subjects in the State List. 2️⃣ Authorizing the creation of new All-India Services. 3️⃣ Certifying a Money Bill.
questions.e: Rajya Sabha has unique powers under Article 249 (State List laws) and Article 312 (All-India Services). Certifying a Money Bill is the *exclusive* power of the Speaker of the Lok Sabha.

questions.q: Parliamentary privileges are NOT extended to which of the following?
questions.e: While the Constitution extends privileges to members, committees, and those entitled to speak (like the Attorney General and Ministers), it explicitly excludes the President, even though he is part of Parliament.

questions.q: What is the difference between "Breach of Privilege" and "Contempt of the House"?
o: They are identical in all legal aspects
Contempt is only for outsiders, while breach is for members
There is no difference; the terms are used interchangeably
A breach of privilege is always contempt, but contempt is not always a breach of privilege
questions.e: Breach of privilege is a violation of specific rights/immunities. Contempt is a broader concept; any act that obstructs the House or lowers its dignity is contempt, even if it doesn't violate a specific privilege.

questions.q: Which of the following factors limits the "Sovereignty" of the Indian Parliament? 1️⃣ Written Nature of the Constitution. 2️⃣ Federal System of Government. 3️⃣ System of Judicial Review.
questions.e: Unlike the British Parliament, the Indian Parliament is not supreme. Its powers are limited by the written Constitution, the division of powers between Center/States, Fundamental Rights, and the power of Courts to review laws.

questions.q: A "Parliamentary Committee" must fulfill which of the following conditions? 1️⃣ It must be appointed/elected by the House or nominated by the Presiding Officer. 2️⃣ It must have a secretariat provided by the Lok Sabha/Rajya Sabha. 3️⃣ It must work under the direction of the President.
questions.e: A committee is "Parliamentary" if it is appointed/elected by the House/Presiding Officer, works under the Presiding Officer's direction, reports to the House/Presiding Officer, and has a secretariat from the House. Consultative Committees don't count.

questions.q: The "Public Accounts Committee" consists of how many members?
questions.e: The PAC consists of 22 members (15 from Lok Sabha and 7 from Rajya Sabha). Its main function is to examine the audit reports of the CAG.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding the "Estimates Committee": 1️⃣ It consists of 30 members. 2️⃣ All its members are from the Lok Sabha only. 3️⃣ Its chairman is always from the Opposition.
questions.e: The Estimates Committee has 30 members, all from the Lok Sabha. Unlike the PAC (where the chairman is usually from the opposition), the chairman of the Estimates Committee is generally from the ruling party.

questions.q: What is the main objective of the "Department-Related Standing Committees" (DRSCs)?
o: To secure more financial accountability of the Executive to Parliament
To advise the President on international treaties
To settle disputes between different political parties
To manage the internal security of the Parliament complex
questions.e: The 24 DRSCs were set up to ensure more detailed scrutiny of the government's spending and policies (accountability), particularly through the examination of demands for grants.

questions.q: The "Indian Parliamentary Group" (IPG) acts as the main branch of which association in India?
questions.e: The IPG is an autonomous body that acts both as the National Group of the Inter-Parliamentary Union (IPU) and the India Branch of the Commonwealth Parliamentary Association (CPA).

questions.q: Who is the ex officio President of the Indian Parliamentary Group?
o: The Speaker of the Lok Sabha
questions.e: The Speaker of the Lok Sabha serves as the ex officio President of the IPG, which promotes relations between the Indian Parliament and other parliaments of the world.

questions.q: Which of the following is TRUE regarding the "Unified Judiciary" in India?
o: Federal laws are enforced by federal courts and state laws by state courts
It was adopted from the American Constitution
The Supreme Court is at the top with High Courts below it
There is no hierarchy of courts below the state level
questions.e: Unlike the USA's dual system, India has a single, integrated (unified) judiciary. Central and state laws are enforced by the same set of courts, with the Supreme Court at the apex.

questions.q: What is the current sanctioned strength of the Supreme Court of India?
questions.e: Originally 8, the number of judges has been increased by Parliament over time. Since 2019, the Supreme Court consists of 34 judges (one Chief Justice and 33 other judges).

questions.q: The "Collegium System" for the appointment of judges: 1️⃣ Was replaced by the NJAC in 2014. 2️⃣ Was restored after the Supreme Court declared the NJAC unconstitutional in 2015. 3️⃣ Requires the CJI to consult four seniormost colleagues for SC appointments.
questions.e: SC/HC judges are appointed via the collegium. The 99th Amendment/NJAC tried to replace it, but the SC struck it down in the Fourth Judges Case (2015). For SC appointments, the CJI must consult a collegium of 4 seniormost judges.

questions.q: What are the qualifications to be appointed as a judge of the Supreme Court? 1️⃣ Citizen of India. 2️⃣ Judge of a High Court for 5 years or Advocate for 10 years. 3️⃣ Minimum age of 45 years.
questions.e: A person must be an Indian citizen and have been a HC judge for 5 years, a HC advocate for 10 years, or a distinguished jurist. Crucially, the Constitution prescribes *no minimum age* for SC judges.

questions.q: A judge of the Supreme Court holds office until he/she attains the age of:
questions.e: While High Court judges retire at 62, Supreme Court judges hold office until the age of 65. They can also resign earlier or be removed by the President.

questions.q: On what grounds can a judge of the Supreme Court be removed?
o: Loss of confidence of the Parliament
questions.e: Article 124(4) states that a judge of the Supreme Court can be removed by the President only on the grounds of "proved misbehaviour or incapacity."

questions.q: Consider the procedure for the removal of a Supreme Court judge: 1️⃣ A removal motion must be signed by 100 members in Lok Sabha. 2️⃣ The motion must be passed by a special majority in both Houses. 3️⃣ No judge has ever been removed by this process in India.
questions.e: Removal requires a motion (100 LS / 50 RS members), an inquiry committee, and a special majority (majority of total + 2/3rd present/voting). While Justice Ramaswami faced the process, the motion failed in the LS; thus, no judge has been successfully removed.

questions.q: When can an "Ad hoc Judge" be appointed to the Supreme Court?
o: To hear cases related to international treaties only
When the President wants to increase the strength of the court
When there is a lack of quorum of permanent judges to hold a session
When the Chief Justice is on leave
questions.e: Under Article 127, the CJI can appoint a High Court judge as an ad hoc judge of the Supreme Court for a temporary period if there is no quorum of SC judges available for a session.

questions.q: The "Original Jurisdiction" of the Supreme Court covers which of the following?
o: Disputes involving private citizens and the Government
Disputes between two or more states
Petitions regarding violation of Fundamental Rights
questions.e: Original jurisdiction (Article 131) means the SC hears the case first. This is limited to federal disputes (Center vs. States or State vs. State). Fundamental Rights fall under Writ Jurisdiction, and HC judgment reviews fall under Appellate Jurisdiction.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT part of the Supreme Court's Original Jurisdiction?
o: Dispute between Center and one or more states
Dispute between two or more states
Dispute where Center and some states are on one side against other states
questions.e: Article 131 explicitly excludes certain matters from original jurisdiction, such as pre-constitution treaties and inter-state river water disputes (governed by separate acts/tribunals).

questions.q: With reference to "Writ Jurisdiction", how does the Supreme Court's power differ from a High Court's?
o: The SC's power is wider than the HC's
The SC can only issue writs for Fundamental Rights, while the HC can issue them for "any other purpose"
The SC can issue writs for any purpose, while the HC is limited to Fundamental Rights
The HC can only issue writs if the SC permits it
questions.e: Under Article 32, the SC's writ jurisdiction is narrower because it's limited to Fundamental Rights. Under Article 226, HCs can issue writs for Fundamental Rights *and* for any other legal right, making their power wider.

questions.q: Under "Advisory Jurisdiction" (Article 143), the Supreme Court:
o: Only hears appeals from military courts
Must give its opinion on any matter referred by the PM
Can refuse to give an opinion on a question of law or fact
Gives opinions that are binding on the President
questions.e: On questions of law/fact, the SC *may* refuse to answer. On pre-constitution treaty disputes, it *must* answer. In all cases, the advice is not binding on the President.

questions.q: What does it mean for the Supreme Court to be a "Court of Record"? 1️⃣ Its judgments are recorded for perpetual memory and testimony. 2️⃣ Its records have evidentiary value and cannot be questioned in any court. 3️⃣ It has the power to punish for contempt of itself.
questions.e: As a Court of Record (Article 129), the SC's proceedings are preserved as legal precedents. It also possesses the power to punish anyone for contempt, which is essential to maintain its dignity.

questions.q: What is "Judicial Review"?
o: The annual report submitted by the CJI to the Parliament
The process of appointing judges to the High Courts
The power of the SC to review its own previous judgments
The power of the judiciary to examine the constitutionality of laws and executive orders
questions.e: Judicial review is the power to check if laws/orders violate the Constitution. If they do (ultra vires), the court can declare them null and void. In India, both the SC and HCs possess this power.

questions.q: Consider the "Scope of Judicial Review" in India vs USA: 1️⃣ India follows "procedure established by law". 2️⃣ USA follows "due process of law". 3️⃣ The scope of judicial review is wider in the USA.
questions.e: In the USA, "due process" allows courts to check both the law's substance and its reasonableness. In India, courts traditionally check only the substantive question (if the authority has the power), though this has evolved. Overall, the USA's scope is considered wider.

questions.q: Which Constitutional Amendment added the "Ninth Schedule" to protect laws from judicial review?
questions.e: The Ninth Schedule was added by the 1st Amendment in 1951 to shield land reform and other laws from being challenged on the grounds of violating fundamental rights.

questions.q: In which landmark case did the Supreme Court rule that laws in the Ninth Schedule are open to challenge if they violate the "Basic Structure"?
questions.e: In the I.R. Coelho case (2007), the SC reaffirmed that no law has blanket immunity. Any law added to the 9th Schedule after April 24, 1973, is subject to judicial review if it violates the basic structure of the Constitution.

questions.q: What is "Judicial Activism"?
o: The strict adherence to judicial precedents
The process where the Executive controls the courts
The proactive role of the judiciary in protecting rights and promoting justice
The system of fast-tracking criminal cases
questions.e: Judicial activism (or judicial dynamism) is when the judiciary takes an assertive role, sometimes departing from precedent or traditional limits, to force the other organs of government to perform their duties.

questions.q: Who among the following were the pioneers of "Public Interest Litigation" (PIL) in India?
o: Justice John Marshall and Justice H.J. Kania
Justice V.R. Krishna Iyer and Justice P.N. Bhagwati
Justice Dipak Misra and Justice Ranjan Gogoi
Justice M.H. Beg and Justice A.N. Ray
questions.e: Introduced in the early 1980s, PIL was pioneered by Justices V.R. Krishna Iyer and P.N. Bhagwati, who relaxed the rule of "locus standi" to allow public-spirited citizens to move the court for the poor.

questions.q: The concept of "Locus Standi" in a traditional sense means:
o: Only the person whose rights are infringed can move the court
Any citizen can move the court for any issue
Lawyers have the exclusive right to speak in court
The court can take up a case on its own (suo motu)
questions.e: Traditionally, only the aggrieved party (the one whose rights were violated) had the "locus standi" (standing) to file a case. PIL is an exception to this rule, allowing third parties to approach the court for the public good.

questions.q: Which of the following will NOT be entertained as a PIL by the Supreme Court?
questions.e: The SC has formulated guidelines on PIL. It will not usually entertain matters related to landlord-tenant disputes, service/pension matters, or medical/educational institution admissions as PILs.

questions.q: What is "Judicial Restraint"?
o: A judicial philosophy where judges limit their own power and defer to the legislature
The process of removing a judge from office
The power of the President to overrule court decisions
A law that prevents judges from taking vacations
questions.e: Judicial restraint is the opposite of activism. It suggests that judges should strictly interpret the law and "original intent," leaving policy-making to elected officials (legislators and executives) and avoiding personal policy preferences.

questions.q: The Constitution of India provides for which pattern of government in the states?
questions.e: The Constitution envisages the same pattern of government for the states as for the Centre, which is the parliamentary system. Part VI of the Constitution (Articles 153 to 167) specifically deals with the state executive.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding the Governor: 1️⃣ He/she is the chief executive head of the state. 2️⃣ He/she acts as an agent of the Central Government. 3️⃣ The same person can be appointed as governor for two or more states.
questions.e: The Governor is the nominal executive head of the state and also functions as a link/agent for the Center. The 7th Amendment Act of 1956 allows one person to serve as Governor for multiple states.

questions.q: How is the Governor of a state appointed?
o: Indirectly elected by the state legislature
Appointed by the President by warrant under his hand and seal
Directly elected by the people of the state
questions.e: The Governor is neither directly nor indirectly elected. He/she is appointed by the President. As held in the Hargovind Pant case (1979), the office is an independent constitutional office, not an employment under the Central Government.

questions.q: Why did India adopt the system of appointment of the Governor rather than direct election? 1️⃣ Direct election is incompatible with the parliamentary system. 2️⃣ It would prevent conflicts between the Governor and the Chief Minister. 3️⃣ It enables the Center to maintain control over the states.
questions.e: The Constituent Assembly chose appointment over election because a constitutional head doesn't need a popular mandate, which could lead to leadership clashes with the CM and foster separatist tendencies. It also aligns with the Canadian model of federalism.

questions.q: Which of the following is a qualification for appointment as a Governor?
o: Must have been a judge of a High Court
Must be a member of the State Legislature
Must have completed the age of 30 years
Must be a citizen of India
questions.e: The Constitution lays down only two qualifications: the person must be a citizen of India and must have completed the age of 35 years.

questions.q: What was a recommendation of the Sarkaria Commission regarding the selection of a Governor?
o: The Vice-President should appoint the Governor
The Governor should be a person from within the state
The Governor should be a detached figure not connected to local politics
The Governor must be a member of the ruling party at the Center
questions.e: The Sarkaria Commission recommended that a Governor should be eminent in some walk of life, be from outside the state, and be a detached figure not too intimately connected with the local politics of the state.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding the Governor's term of office: 1️⃣ A Governor holds office for a term of five years from the date he enters office. 2️⃣ The Governor's term is subject to the pleasure of the President. 3️⃣ The Supreme Court held in the Surya Narain case that the pleasure of the President is not justifiable.
questions.e: Article 156 states the Governor holds office for five years subject to the President's pleasure. The Supreme Court in the Surya Narain case (1981) ruled that the Governor has no security of tenure and the President's pleasure is not justifiable in court.

questions.q: Which of the following is correct regarding the conditions of the Governor's office? 1️⃣ He/she should not be a member of either House of Parliament or a House of the state legislature. 2️⃣ His/her emoluments and allowances can be diminished during the term of office in case of a financial emergency. 3️⃣ He/she is entitled to the use of his official residence without payment of rent.
questions.e: The Governor cannot be a member of Parliament or state legislature; if such a person is appointed, they vacate their seat on the date of entering office. While emoluments are determined by Parliament, they cannot be diminished during the term of office. The Governor is entitled to rent-free use of the Raj Bhavan.

questions.q: In case of the death of a sitting Governor, who among the following may be appointed temporarily by the President to discharge the functions of the Governor?
o: The Chief Justice of the concerned State High Court
The Speaker of the State Legislative Assembly
The Chief Minister of the State
questions.e: The President can make provisions for contingencies not provided in the Constitution. For example, if a Governor dies in office, the Chief Justice of the concerned state high court may be appointed temporarily to discharge those functions.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT an executive power of the Governor?
o: Appointment of the State Advocate General
Removal of the members of the State Public Service Commission
Appointment of the Chairman of the State Public Service Commission
Appointment of the State Election Commissioner
questions.e: The Governor appoints the chairman and members of the State Public Service Commission, but they can only be removed by the President, not the Governor. The Governor does appoint the Advocate General and the State Election Commissioner.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding the Governor’s legislative powers: 1️⃣ He/she can summon or prorogue the state legislature and dissolve the state legislative assembly. 2️⃣ He/she nominates one-twelfth of the members of the state legislative council. 3️⃣ He/she can promulgate ordinances only when the state legislature is not in session.
questions.e: The Governor summons/prorogues the legislature and can dissolve the assembly. He/she nominates one-sixth (not one-twelfth) of the legislative council members. Ordinances are promulgated when the legislature is in recess and have the same force as an act.

questions.q: When a bill is sent to the Governor after being passed by the state legislature, he/she can: 1️⃣ Give assent to the bill. 2️⃣ Withhold assent to the bill. 3️⃣ Return the bill (if not a money bill) for reconsideration. 4️⃣ Reserve the bill for the consideration of the President.
questions.e: Under Article 200, the Governor has four alternatives: grant assent, withhold assent, return the bill for reconsideration (if it's an ordinary bill), or reserve it for the President.

questions.q: In which of the following cases is it "obligatory" for the Governor to reserve a bill for the consideration of the President?
o: If the bill is opposed to the Directive Principles of State Policy
If the bill endangers the position of the State High Court
If the bill deals with the compulsory acquisition of property
If the bill is of grave national importance
questions.e: While the Governor can reserve various types of bills, reservation is mandatory if a bill passed by the state legislature endangers the position or powers of the state high court.

questions.q: An ordinance promulgated by the Governor ceases to operate on the expiry of ________ from the reassembly of the state legislature.
questions.e: Every ordinance issued by the Governor must be approved by the state legislature within six weeks of its reassembly, or it ceases to operate.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding the Governor's pardoning powers under Article 161: 1️⃣ He/she can grant pardons to any person convicted of an offence against a state law. 2️⃣ He/she has the power to pardon a death sentence if the state law prescribes it. 3️⃣ He/she cannot grant pardon in respect of a punishment by a court-martial.
questions.e: The Governor can pardon offences against state laws. However, only the President can pardon a death sentence; the Governor can only suspend, remit, or commute it. The Governor possesses no power regarding court-martial sentences.

questions.q: Which of the following constitutional provisions describes the "Constitutional Discretion" of the Governor? 1️⃣ Recommendation for the imposition of President’s Rule. 2️⃣ Reservation of a bill for the consideration of the President. 3️⃣ Appointment of Chief Minister when no party has a clear majority.
questions.e: Constitutional discretion includes reservation of bills and recommending President's rule. Situational discretion (hidden discretion) applies to the appointment of a CM in a hung assembly or when a CM dies suddenly.

questions.q: For which of the following states does the Governor have a "special responsibility" to establish separate development boards for specific regions?
questions.e: The Governor has special responsibilities under the direction of the President for establishing development boards in Maharashtra (Vidarbha, Marathwada) and Gujarat (Saurashtra, Kutch).

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding "Situational Discretion" of the Governor: 1️⃣ Dismissal of the council of ministers when it cannot prove confidence. 2️⃣ Dissolution of the state legislative assembly if the council has lost its majority. 3️⃣ Appointment of the Chief Minister when there is no obvious successor.
questions.e: Situational discretion arises from political exigencies, such as appointing a CM in a hung assembly, dismissing a ministry that lost confidence, or dissolving the assembly when the majority is lost.

questions.q: According to the Sarkaria Commission, what should be the procedure for appointing a Governor to ensure effective consultation?
o: The Chief Minister should have the final power of veto over the appointment
The President should act solely on the advice of the Vice-President
The Governor should be elected by the State Legislature
The procedure of consultation with the State Chief Minister should be prescribed in the Constitution
questions.e: The Sarkaria Commission recommended that to ensure effective consultation with the state CM, the procedure should be codified by amending Article 155.

questions.q: Which Article of the Constitution deals with the "Conduct of business of the government of a state"?
questions.e: Article 166 specifies that all executive actions of the state government shall be taken in the name of the Governor and deals with the rules of business.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding the Governor as Chancellor: 1️⃣ He/she acts as the chancellor of universities in the state. 2️⃣ In his capacity as Chancellor, he/she must abide by the advice of the Council of Ministers. 3️⃣ He/she appoints the vice-chancellors of universities in the state.
questions.e: The Governor is the ex-officio Chancellor of state universities and appoints Vice-Chancellors. However, as Chancellor, he/she acts under university statutes rather than constitutional advice, a point often debated.

questions.q: Which of the following pair(s) is/are correctly matched? 1️⃣ Article 153: Governors of states. 2️⃣ Article 161: Pardoning power of Governor. 3️⃣ Article 213: Power of Governor to promulgate ordinances.
questions.e: Article 153 provides for Governors. Article 161 confers the power to grant pardons and reprieves. Article 213 empowers the Governor to issue ordinances when the legislature is in recess.

questions.q: The Governor’s "Pardoning Power" under Article 161 differs from the President’s power under Article 72 because:
o: The President cannot commute a sentence
The Governor can only pardon civil offences
The Governor cannot pardon a death sentence
The Governor's power is absolute and not subject to judicial review
questions.e: While both can suspend or commute a death sentence, the President is the *only* authority who can grant a full pardon for a death sentence.

questions.q: With reference to the state budget, what is the role of the Governor?
o: He/she sees that the Annual Financial Statement is laid before the state legislature
He/she prepares the budget and presents it to the assembly
He/she can withdraw money from the Consolidated Fund without an appropriation bill
He/she has the power to increase any demand for a grant
questions.e: Under the financial powers of the Governor, he/she ensures the "Annual Financial Statement" (budget) is laid before the state legislature.

questions.q: Consider the following statements: 1️⃣ A person can be appointed as a Governor for two or more states. 2️⃣ The Governor is an employee of the Central Government. 3️⃣ The office of Governor is an independent constitutional office.
questions.e: The 7th Amendment (1956) allows a Governor for multiple states. The Supreme Court in the Hargovind Pant case (1979) ruled the office is an independent constitutional post, not central government employment.

questions.q: Which of the following is a "Situational Discretion" of the Governor as identified by the Sarkaria Commission?
o: Appointment of the State Election Commissioner
Reservation of a bill for the President's consideration
Prorogation of the state legislature session
Dismissal of a Chief Minister who refuses to resign after losing majority support
questions.e: The Commission noted that the Governor must exercise discretion in dismissing a CM who refuses to resign or face the house after clearly losing majority support.

questions.q: Who provides the secretariat for a Parliamentary Committee?
o: The Lok Sabha or Rajya Sabha
questions.e: One of the four conditions for a committee to be "Parliamentary" is that it must have a secretariat provided by the Lok Sabha or Rajya Sabha.

questions.q: The "Public Accounts Committee" (PAC) was first established in which year?
questions.e: The PAC was first set up in 1921 under the provisions of the Government of India Act of 1919 and has been in existence ever since.

questions.q: Which of the following statements regarding the "Public Accounts Committee" is incorrect?
o: 15 members are from Lok Sabha and 7 from Rajya Sabha
The chairman is usually selected from the Opposition
A Minister can be a member of the committee
questions.e: A minister cannot be elected as a member of the Public Accounts Committee. All other statements are correct.

questions.q: The "Estimates Committee" is known as:
o: The guardian of the public purse
questions.e: The Estimates Committee is described as a "continuous economy committee" because its function is to suggest 'economies' in public expenditure by suggesting administrative reforms or alternative policies.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding the "Committee on Public Undertakings": 1️⃣ It was created in 1964 on the recommendation of the Krishna Menon Committee. 2️⃣ It consists of 30 members. 3️⃣ It examines whether the affairs of public undertakings are managed according to sound business principles.
questions.e: The committee was created in 1964. It currently has 22 members (raised from 15 in 1974), not 30. Its function is to examine the efficiency and business management of public undertakings.

questions.q: How many "Department-Related Standing Committees" (DRSCs) are currently functional in the Indian Parliament?
questions.e: Initially 17 DRSCs were set up in 1993; in 2004, seven more were added, bringing the total to 24.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding the composition of DRSCs: 1️⃣ Each committee consists of 31 members. 2️⃣ 21 members are from Lok Sabha and 10 from Rajya Sabha. 3️⃣ Members are nominated by the Speaker/Chairman.
questions.e: Each of the 24 DRSCs has 31 members (21 from LS, 10 from RS). The LS members are nominated by the Speaker, and RS members by the Chairman.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a function of the Department-Related Standing Committees?
o: To examine bills pertaining to the concerned ministries
To consider annual reports of ministries
To consider the matters of day-to-day administration
questions.e: DRSCs are specifically restricted from considering matters of day-to-day administration of the concerned ministries/departments.

questions.q: Which committee classifies bills and allocates time for the discussion on bills introduced by private members in the Lok Sabha?
o: Committee on Private Members' Bills and Resolutions
questions.e: The Committee on Private Members' Bills and Resolutions is a special committee of the Lok Sabha that manages time and classification for non-government bills.

questions.q: The "Joint Committee on Salaries and Allowances of Members of Parliament" was constituted under which Act?
o: The Salaries and Allowances of Ministers Act, 1952
The Salary, Allowances and Pension of Members of Parliament Act, 1954
questions.e: This committee consists of 15 members and was established under the Salary, Allowances and Pension of Members of Parliament Act, 1954.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding "Consultative Committees": 1️⃣ They are formal Parliamentary Committees. 2️⃣ They are constituted by the Ministry of Parliamentary Affairs. 3️⃣ Membership is voluntary.
questions.e: Consultative committees are *not* parliamentary committees because they don't fulfill the standard criteria. They are constituted by the Ministry of Parliamentary Affairs with voluntary membership.

questions.q: Who acts as the "guide, friend and philosopher" of the Public Accounts Committee?
questions.e: In the fulfillment of its functions (examining audit reports), the PAC is assisted by the CAG, who acts as its guide, friend, and philosopher.

questions.q: The "Committee on Subordinate Legislation" was first constituted in which year?
questions.e: The Committee on Subordinate Legislation, which checks if delegated powers are being properly exercised, was constituted in 1953.

questions.q: Which committee examines petitions on bills and matters of general public importance?
questions.e: The Committee on Petitions examines petitions on bills and representations from individuals on Union subjects.

questions.q: The "Ethics Committee" was first constituted in the Rajya Sabha in which year?
questions.e: The Ethics Committee was constituted in the Rajya Sabha in 1997 and later in the Lok Sabha in 2000 to enforce the code of conduct for members.

questions.q: Which of the following correctly describes "Ad Hoc Committees"?
o: Committees consisting only of Rajya Sabha members
Committees concerned only with financial matters
Temporary committees that cease to exist on completion of a task
questions.e: Ad hoc committees are temporary and cease to exist once they complete their assigned task, such as Inquiry Committees or Advisory Committees on bills.

questions.q: The "General Purposes Committee" is headed by:
o: The Presiding Officer of the House (Speaker/Chairman)
questions.e: In each House, the General Purposes Committee consists of the presiding officer as its ex-officio chairman.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding "Library Committee": 1️⃣ It consists of 9 members. 2️⃣ 6 members are from Lok Sabha and 3 from Rajya Sabha. 3️⃣ It is a permanent standing committee.
questions.e: The Library Committee is a house-keeping/service committee consisting of 9 members (6 LS, 3 RS) that assists members in using library services.

questions.q: Which committee deals with residential accommodation and amenities like medical aid for members of Parliament?
questions.e: The House Committee deals with the residential accommodation and amenities like food and medical aid for members in Delhi.

questions.q: The "Indian Parliamentary Group" (IPG) was formed in which year?
questions.e: The IPG is an autonomous body formed in 1949 in pursuance of a motion adopted by the Constituent Assembly (Legislative).

questions.q: Who among the following can become an "Associate Member" of the Indian Parliamentary Group?
questions.e: While membership is open to all sitting MPs, former MPs can become associate members with limited rights.

questions.q: The "Outstanding Parliamentarian Award" was instituted by the IPG in which year?
questions.e: As per a decision of the IPG, the award of Outstanding Parliamentarian was instituted in 1995 to be given annually.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT an objective of the "Indian Parliamentary Group"?
o: To study questions of public importance
To arrange lectures on political and economic problems
To promote personal contact between members of Parliament
To settle disputes between the Centre and States
questions.e: The IPG focuses on inter-parliamentary relations and contact between members; it does not have the authority to settle center-state disputes.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding "Parliamentary Friendship Groups" (PFGs): 1️⃣ They are constituted by the IPG. 2️⃣ The Speaker of Lok Sabha appoints the President of each PFG. 3️⃣ They consist of members from both Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha.
questions.e: PFGs are created by the IPG to encourage bilateral relations; they are composed of sitting MPs from both houses and have presidents appointed by the Speaker.

questions.q: The "Inter-Parliamentary Union" (IPU) currently consists of how many parliaments?
questions.e: At present, the IPU consists of 179 parliaments of sovereign nations, working for peace and cooperation among peoples.

questions.q: The "Commonwealth Parliamentary Association" (CPA) includes about how many Parliamentarians?
questions.e: The CPA is an association of about 17,000 Parliamentarians and staff spread over 180 legislatures in 53 Commonwealth countries.

questions.q: Which publication is provided free of charge to all members of the IPG by the CPA?
questions.e: Members are entitled to receive 'The Parliamentarian' (quarterly) and the newsletter 'First Reading' (every second month).

questions.q: Who is the ex-officio "Secretary-General" of the Indian Parliamentary Group?
questions.e: The Secretary-General of the Lok Sabha acts as the ex-officio Secretary-General of the IPG.

questions.q: When was the Supreme Court of India inaugurated?
questions.e: The Supreme Court was inaugurated on January 28, 1950, succeeding the Federal Court of India established under the 1935 Act.

questions.q: Originally, the strength of the Supreme Court was fixed at:
questions.e: Originally, the strength was fixed at eight (one Chief Justice and seven other judges).

questions.q: Which Article of the Constitution deals with the "Appointment of Judges" of the Supreme Court?
questions.e: Article 124 deals with the establishment and constitution of the Supreme Court, including the appointment of judges.

questions.q: In the "Second Judges Case" (1993), the Supreme Court ruled that:
o: The President has absolute discretion in appointments
The advice of the Chief Justice of India is binding on the President
The Collegium must consist of all Supreme Court judges
questions.e: In 1993, the court reversed its earlier ruling and held that "consultation" means "concurrence," making the CJI's advice binding on the President.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding the "Collegium System" for SC appointments as per the Third Judges Case (1998): 1️⃣ The CJI should consult a collegium of four seniormost judges. 2️⃣ If two judges give an adverse opinion, the CJI should not send the recommendation. 3️⃣ The opinion of the CJI alone constitutes the consultation process.
questions.e: The court ruled that plurality of judges is required; the CJI must consult 4 senior colleagues. If two give an adverse opinion, the recommendation should not be sent.

questions.q: Which Constitutional Amendment Act attempted to replace the Collegium system with the "National Judicial Appointments Commission" (NJAC)?
questions.e: The 99th Constitutional Amendment Act of 2014 tried to replace the collegium with the NJAC, but it was declared unconstitutional in 2015.

questions.q: In 1973, who was appointed as the Chief Justice of India by superseding three senior judges?
questions.e: A.N. Ray was appointed in 1973, violating the convention of appointing the seniormost judge. This was due to the superseded judges' ruling in the Kesavananda Bharati case.

questions.q: To be appointed as a judge of the Supreme Court, an advocate of a High Court must have practiced for at least:
questions.e: One of the qualifications is being an advocate of a High Court (or courts in succession) for at least ten years.

questions.q: Who administers the "Oath or Affirmation" to a judge of the Supreme Court?
o: The President or some person appointed by him
questions.e: Before entering office, a judge must swear an oath before the President or his appointee.

questions.q: The salaries and allowances of Supreme Court judges are determined by:
questions.e: Article 125 provides that salaries, allowances, and pensions are determined from time to time by the Parliament.

questions.q: A judge of the Supreme Court can be removed by the President only after an address by Parliament supported by:
o: Special majority (2/3rd of members present and voting + majority of total strength)
questions.e: Removal requires an address supported by a majority of the total membership and a majority of not less than two-thirds of the members present and voting.

questions.q: Who was the first judge of the Supreme Court to face "impeachment" proceedings?
questions.e: Justice V. Ramaswami (1991-1993) was the first. Though guilty of misbehaviour, the motion was defeated in Lok Sabha because the Congress Party abstained.

questions.q: The "Ad hoc Judge" appointed to the Supreme Court must be:
o: A distinguished jurist appointed by the PM
A judge of a High Court qualified for SC appointment
A member of the Law Commission
questions.e: The CJI can appoint a High Court judge as an ad hoc judge if they are qualified to be an SC judge, provided there is a lack of quorum.

questions.q: Which Article of the Constitution authorizes the "Chief Justice of India" to request a retired judge to act as an SC judge?
questions.e: Under Article 128, the CJI can request a retired SC or HC judge to act as an SC judge for a temporary period with the President's consent.

questions.q: The "Constitutional Cases" or references made by the President under Article 143 are decided by a Bench of at least:
questions.e: Cases involving interpretation of the Constitution or Presidential references must be heard by a bench of at least five judges.

questions.q: Why are the "Administrative Expenses" of the Supreme Court non-votable by Parliament?
o: Because they are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India
Because they are paid by the States
Because the Parliament has no right to discuss them
questions.e: Salaries, pensions, and administrative expenses are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India to ensure judicial independence, making them non-votable.

questions.q: Which of the following is an "Exclusive Original Jurisdiction" of the Supreme Court?
o: Disputes between the Centre and one or more states
Disputes between a citizen and the State
Matters referred to the Finance Commission
questions.e: Exclusive original jurisdiction (Article 131) covers federal disputes like Center vs. States or State vs. State.

questions.q: The Supreme Court’s "Writ Jurisdiction" for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights is:
questions.e: It is "original" because a citizen can go directly to the SC, but "not exclusive" because High Courts also have this power under Article 226.

questions.q: In which year did the Parliament enlarge the "Criminal Appellate Jurisdiction" of the Supreme Court?
questions.e: In 1970, Parliament expanded the right to appeal to cases where a HC reversed an acquittal and sentenced a person to life imprisonment or 10 years.

questions.q: Under "Appeal by Special Leave" (Article 136), the Supreme Court can grant leave against:
o: Any court or tribunal except military ones
questions.e: Article 136 is very wide; it covers any matter (civil, criminal, etc.) from any court or tribunal, except military ones, and applies to both final and interlocutory orders.

questions.q: How many "Presidential References" have been made to the Supreme Court under its Advisory Jurisdiction so far?
questions.e: According to the text, the President has made fifteen references to the Supreme Court under Article 143.

questions.q: The "Contempt of Courts Act" was enacted in which year?
questions.e: Based on the Sanyal Committee report, the Parliament enacted the Contempt of Courts Act in 1971.

questions.q: "Judicial Review" power of the Supreme Court allows it to:
o: Appoint the members of the UPSC
Advise the PM on legal matters
Examine the constitutionality of legislative enactments and executive orders
questions.e: Judicial review is the power to check if Central or State laws/orders violate the Constitution; if they do, the court declares them null and void.

questions.q: A "Review Petition" must be filed within how many days from the date of the judgment?
questions.e: The Supreme Court has the power to review its own judgments; a petition for this must be filed within thirty days.

questions.q: Consider the following "Doctrines" applied by the Supreme Court in interpreting the Constitution: 1️⃣ Doctrine of Severability. 2️⃣ Doctrine of Pith and Substance. 3️⃣ Doctrine of Colourable Legislation.
questions.e: All three are important doctrines used by the court to determine the validity of laws and the competence of legislatures.

questions.q: Which Article states that the "Law declared by the Supreme Court" shall be binding on all courts in India?
questions.e: Under Article 141, the law laid down by the Supreme Court is binding on all other courts within the territory of India.

questions.q: Who propounded the doctrine of "Judicial Review" for the first time?
questions.e: The doctrine originated in the USA and was first propounded in the Marbury vs. Madison case (1803) by Chief Justice John Marshall.

questions.q: In India, "Judicial Review" is considered:
o: A temporary power granted by the PM
A basic feature of the Constitution
A power only for the Lok Sabha
questions.e: The Supreme Court has declared that judicial review is a "basic feature" or element of the "basic structure," meaning it cannot be removed even by constitutional amendment.

questions.q: "Judicial Review" can be classified into which of the following categories? 1️⃣ Review of constitutional amendments. 2️⃣ Review of legislation. 3️⃣ Review of administrative action.
questions.e: Justice Syed Shah Mohamed Quadri classified judicial review into these three specific categories.

questions.q: Which case established that laws in the "Ninth Schedule" added after April 24, 1973, are subject to judicial review?
questions.e: In the I.R. Coelho case (2007), the court ruled that there is no blanket immunity for laws in the Ninth Schedule and they must be tested against fundamental rights and basic structure.

questions.q: The term "Judicial Activism" was first coined by:
questions.e: The term was coined in 1947 by Arthur Schlesinger Jr., an American historian, in a magazine article.

questions.q: "Judicial Activism" is often described as the antithesis of:
questions.e: Judicial activism (proactive role) is the opposite of judicial restraint (self-control and limited interference).

questions.q: Which of the following are "Activators" of judicial activism in India as per Upendra Baxi? 1️⃣ Consumer Rights Groups. 2️⃣ Bonded Labour Groups. 3️⃣ Indigenous People’s Rights Groups.
questions.e: Baxi identified various groups like child rights, custodial rights, and poverty rights activists as triggers for the court's proactive role.

questions.q: "Judicial Restraint" philosophy suggests that judges should:
o: Leave the business of law-making to legislators
Avoid interpreting the "original intent" of authors
Base decisions on personal political values
questions.e: Restraint advocates believe the role of judges is limited to saying what the law *is*, leaving law-making to elected officials.

questions.q: The concept of "Public Interest Litigation" (PIL) originated in which country?
questions.e: PIL originated in the USA in the 1960s to provide legal representation to unrepresented groups like the poor and minorities.

questions.q: "PIL" is also known as: 1️⃣ Social Action Litigation (SAL). 2️⃣ Social Interest Litigation (SIL). 3️⃣ Class Action Litigation (CAL).
questions.e: In India, PIL is variously known as SAL, SIL, or CAL.

questions.q: The relaxation of which traditional rule facilitated the introduction of PIL in India?
questions.e: Traditionally, only an aggrieved person could move court. PIL relaxed the "locus standi" rule, allowing any public-spirited citizen to move the court for the disadvantaged.

questions.q: Which of the following is a "Feature" of PIL?
o: It is strictly for wealthy litigants
It is a co-operative effort between the petitioner, State, and Court
questions.e: PIL is not a traditional dispute between two parties; it is a collaborative effort to secure constitutional rights for vulnerable sections.

questions.q: Petitions falling under which of the following categories will be entertained as PIL? 1️⃣ Bonded labour matters. 2️⃣ Neglected children. 3️⃣ Service matters pertaining to pension.
questions.e: Guidelines specify that bonded labour, neglected children, and pollution matters are valid PILs. However, service matters and landlord-tenant disputes are NOT entertained as PILs.

questions.q: What is the meaning of "Res Judicata"?
o: The standing of a litigant in court
The power of the court to issue writs
A matter that has been finally adjudicated upon and cannot be reopened
questions.e: Res judicata is the legal principle that once a case is finally decided by a competent court, it cannot be reopened by the same parties.

questions.q: The Supreme Court warned against the misuse of PIL, referring to it as: 1️⃣ Publicity Interest Litigation. 2️⃣ Politics Interest Litigation. 3️⃣ Paisa Interest Litigation.
questions.e: The court cautioned that PIL should not be used for personal gain, private motives, or publicity (MIL/MIL/PIL).

questions.q: According to Article 154, the "Executive Power" of the State is vested in:
questions.e: Article 154 explicitly states that the executive power of the state is vested in the Governor and is exercised by him directly or through subordinate officers.

questions.q: The "foundation" of the parliamentary system of government in the states is provided by which Article?
questions.e: Article 164, which states that the council of ministers is collectively responsible to the state assembly, is the core of the parliamentary system at the state level.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding the Governor’s "Discretionary Powers": 1️⃣ The Constitution envisages the possibility of the Governor acting in his discretion. 2️⃣ No such possibility of discretionary action is envisaged for the President. 3️⃣ The Governor's decision on whether a matter falls within his discretion is final.
questions.e: Unlike the President, the Governor has both constitutional and situational discretion. His decision on the use of discretion cannot be questioned.

questions.q: In which case did the Supreme Court hold that the Governor’s office is an "Independent Constitutional Office"?
questions.e: In the Hargovind Pant vs. Raghukul Tilak case (1979), the court ruled the Governor is not a subordinate to the Central Government.

questions.q: The "94th Constitutional Amendment Act" (2006) excluded which state from the requirement of having a Tribal Welfare Minister?
questions.e: The states of Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, MP, and Odisha must have a Tribal Welfare Minister; Bihar was excluded from this list in 2006.

questions.q: A Governor can be "removed" from office at any time by:
questions.e: The Governor holds office during the pleasure of the President, who can remove him at any time without laying down grounds.

questions.q: When the same person is appointed as Governor for two states, how is their "Salary" shared?
o: Shared in a proportion determined by the President
Shared equally between the two states
Paid by the state where the Governor resides most
questions.e: Under the conditions of office, the emoluments are shared by the states in a proportion determined by the President.

questions.q: Consider the following "Legislative Powers" of the Governor: 1️⃣ He/she can address the state legislature at the first session of each general election. 2️⃣ He/she can send messages to the house regarding a pending bill. 3️⃣ He/she appoints the Speaker of the assembly in case of a vacancy.
questions.e: The Governor addresses the first session and can send messages. However, if the office of Speaker is vacant, the Governor *appoints a member* to preside until a new Speaker is elected, rather than "appointing the Speaker" permanently.

questions.q: Which Article deals with "Assent to bills" by the Governor?
questions.e: Article 200 details the options available to a Governor when a bill is passed by the state legislature.

questions.q: What happens if the President returns a "State Bill" for reconsideration and the House passes it again?
o: The President is bound to give assent
The Governor can then give assent
The President is not bound to give assent
questions.e: Unlike Central bills (where the President must give assent after reconsideration), in the case of a state bill, the President is *not* bound to give assent even if it is passed again by the state house.

questions.q: "Situational Discretion" of the Governor includes:
o: Determining the royalty for mineral exploration
Dismissing a council of ministers that lost majority but refuses to resign
Nominating members to the State Legislative Council
questions.e: Situational discretion refers to actions taken based on political circumstances, such as dismissing a ministry that no longer has the house's confidence.

questions.q: Which of the following is true regarding the "Rules of Procedure" of Parliamentary Committees?
o: They are mentioned in detail in Article 105
They are fixed by the President
They are decided by the Prime Minister
They are dealt with by the rules of the two Houses
questions.e: While the Constitution mentions committees, it does not provide specific rules for composition or functions; these are managed by the rules of the Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha.
